faq.a: Yes; secondary infection can lead to cellulitis or septic arthritis and requires antibiotics and drainage.
faq.q: Can a Baker cyst become infected?

faq.a: Flexion increases intra‑articular pressure, pushing more synovial fluid into the popliteal bursa.
faq.q: Why does the cyst enlarge when the knee is flexed?

faq.a: No; most cysts resolve with treatment of the underlying joint disease and conservative measures.

exam: What bedside maneuver helps differentiate a Baker cyst from DVT? — Gentle knee flexion makes the cyst enlarge; DVT remains unchanged.
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a painful posterior knee mass. What is your next step? — Perform bedside ultrasound to confirm cystic nature before considering aspiration.

How would you manage a ruptured Baker cyst that mimics DVT in a setting without Doppler ultrasound? — Assess calf tenderness, check for Homan’s sign, obtain a limited ultrasound if possible; if unavailable, treat as possible DVT with anticoagulation while arranging referral.
Why are intra‑articular steroids contraindicated in a suspected septic knee? — Steroids suppress immune response and can worsen infection; obtain synovial fluid analysis first.
List three physiotherapy measures that reduce cyst recurrence. — Quadriceps strengthening, hamstring stretching, avoidance of prolonged knee flexion.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent imaging in a patient with a known Baker cyst? — New onset calf pain with swelling and warmth suggesting rupture or compartment syndrome.
Explain why a popliteal artery aneurysm must be excluded before cyst aspiration. — An aneurysm is pulsatile and can bleed catastrophically if punctured.
In a patient with HIV and knee effusion, what additional cause should you consider? — Tuberculous arthritis, which can produce large effusions and secondary cysts.
ai.title: Popliteal (Baker) Cyst
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A Baker cyst is a synovial fluid‑filled popliteal sac that develops secondary to knee joint effusion. It presents with posterior knee swelling and can mimic DVT if ruptured.

b: Palpable, fluctuant mass behind the knee, often enlarges with knee flexion
Transillumination may be positive if fluid‑filled
Ultrasound or bedside limited musculoskeletal scan confirms cystic nature
sections.p: A Baker cyst is a synovial-lined pouch that protrudes into the popliteal fossa when excess knee joint fluid is forced into the gastrocnemio‑semimembranosus bursa.

b: Stage I – Small (<3 cm), asymptomatic
Stage II – Moderate (3–6 cm), pain on flexion, limited ROM
Stage III – Large (>6 cm) or ruptured, calf swelling, possible DVT‑like signs
sections.p: Severity is graded by size, symptom burden and presence of rupture or neurovascular compromise.

b: Rheumatoid arthritis – most common inflammatory cause
Osteoarthritis of the knee – degenerative effusion
Post‑traumatic meniscal tear or ligament injury
Seronegative spondyloarthropathies (e.g., reactive arthritis)
In low‑resource settings: septic arthritis, tuberculous knee, HIV‑related arthropathy
sections.p: The cyst is almost always secondary to intra‑articular pathology that drives excess synovial fluid.

b: Posterior knee fullness, often unilateral
Pain worsens with knee extension or activity
If ruptured: sudden calf pain, swelling, mimicking DVT
Reduced knee flexion range of motion
sections.p: Patients notice a swelling behind the knee that may be painful, especially when the knee is fully extended or after prolonged standing.
Focused bedside tools are preferred where imaging is limited.

t.b: Distinguishes cyst from DVT or calf tear; a firm, non‑pulsatile mass that enlarges with knee flexion favours cyst
Answers whether the swelling is cystic or thrombotic; an anechoic, well‑defined structure with posterior acoustic enhancement confirms cyst
Helps identify underlying inflammatory or septic arthritis; cloudy fluid with high leukocytes suggests infection
Shows osteoarthritic changes or bony fragments that may explain effusion

b: Rupture → calf compartment syndrome, mimics DVT
Infection of cyst → cellulitis, septic arthritis
Neurovascular compression → foot numbness, venous stasis
sections.p: Complications are rare but can be serious, especially when misdiagnosed as DVT.

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for pain and inflammation – avoid in active peptic ulcer disease
Intra‑articular corticosteroid injection for inflammatory effusion – avoid if infection suspected
Physiotherapy: quadriceps strengthening, gentle knee flexion/extension exercises
Aspiration of large cysts only if symptomatic and sterile technique can be ensured
Surgical excision or arthroscopic cyst decompression for recurrent or ruptured cysts when conservative measures fail
sections.p: Treat the underlying knee pathology first, then address the cyst itself.

b: Re‑evaluate knee effusion every 4–6 weeks after initiating therapy
Educate patient on avoiding prolonged knee flexion and heavy squatting
Monitor for signs of infection or recurrence, especially in immunocompromised patients
sections.p: Regular review of knee joint status prevents recurrence.

b: Deep vein thrombosis – distinguished by ultrasound Doppler and lack of cystic appearance
Calf muscle tear – history of acute trauma, focal tenderness over muscle belly
Popliteal artery aneurysm – pulsatile mass, audible bruit
sections.p: Several conditions present with posterior knee or calf swelling.

b: Normal D‑dimer does not exclude a ruptured cyst mimicking DVT
Ultrasound may miss a small cyst if probe pressure collapses it; repeat with gentle technique
sections.p: Certain investigations may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden calf swelling with pain and warmth – rule out DVT or compartment syndrome
Fever, redness, or rapidly enlarging mass – suspect infection
Neurological deficit (foot drop, numbness) – possible neurovascular compression
